sections.html:
The Taiwan banded barb, Acrossocheilus paradoxus, is a cyprinid native to Taiwan, where it occurs throughout western and northeastern river drainages. It inhabits subtropical streams and small to medium rivers at medium to relatively high altitudes, and in the aquarium needs spotless, well-oxygenated water with moderate flow. Growing to around 200 mm SL, it needs a tank of at least 180 x 45 cm.

  • Max size: 200 mm SL (8 in SL)
  • Aquarium size: 180 × 45 cm (72 × 18 in)
  • Temperature: 15–25°C (59–77°F)
  • pH: 6.0–8.0
  • Hardness: 2–12 dGH

A medium-sized barbel native to China and Taiwan that only rarely reaches the hobby. In the wild specimens are usually up to 12 cm total length, but the record is 22.5 cm. Such large animals look different: the head is longer and the banded pattern gives way to a uniform green-golden shine.

Native to Taiwan, where it occurs throughout western and northeastern river drainages, plus Fujian and Zhejiang provinces, mainland China. No specific type locality is provided in Günther's description.
Inhabits subtropical streams and small-to-medium sized rivers at medium to relatively high altitudes.
In nature this subtropical species lives in boulder-filled rivers, which resemble smaller alpine rivers in their structure.
An aquarium with base dimensions of 180 × 45 cm (72 × 18 in) or equivalent (about 365 litres) should be the smallest considered for long-term maintenance.

Likely to prefer a set-up designed to resemble a flowing river with a substrate of variably-sized rocks and gravel and some large water-worn boulders. This can be further furnished with driftwood roots and branches arranged to form some shaded spots.

While the vast majority of plant species will fail to thrive in such surroundings hardy types such as Microsorum, Bolbitis or Anubias can be grown attached to the décor and bright lighting will promote the growth of aufwuchs upon which the fish will graze.

Like many fishes that naturally inhabit running water it is intolerant to the accumulation of organic wastes and requires spotless conditions in order to thrive, meaning weekly water changes of 30-50% tank volume should be considered routine. Though torrent-like conditions are unnecessary it also does best if there is a high level of dissolved oxygen and moderate water movement.

Since it doesn't cope well with fluctuating water conditions try to acclimatise it to the aquarium over a couple of hours if possible, and it should never be introduced to a biologically immature system.

Regarding the water composition A. paradoxus is undemanding. Since the water temperatures in the home waters of the species can sink under 15°C in the winter, it should be kept occasionally cool with reduced lighting.
Wild fish are known to feed on small, benthic invertebrates and graze biofilm from rocks and other solid surfaces.

The mouth has a horny layer at the front edge, which probably serves to rasp off growth from the rock. In addition, A. paradoxus has two well developed barbels, which are used for detecting small animals in the sand.

In behavior Acrossocheilus paradoxus resembles other algae-eating barbels, like Garra or sharks (Labeo and allies). Among themselves they can be a bit quarrelsome.
With cool keeping and reduced lighting, breeding should also be possible, but none has been reported yet. One can assume that it is a free spawner without special brood care.

The genus Acrossocheilus is restricted to southern China, Taiwan, northern Vietnam and northern Laos. It can be distinguished from related genera by the following combination of characters: rostral fold present; lips fleshy and continuous around corners of mouth; lower lip with a median interruption; mouth inferior; horny sheath on lower jaw; two pairs of barbels; last simple ray of dorsal fin osseous with a serrated or smooth posterior margin.

Members of the genus are characterised by possessing a particular number of dark vertical bar on each flank, and A. paradoxus belongs to a group of species with five or six such bars, each of which is two scales in width. Congeners sharing this pattern include A. fasciatus, A. hemispinus (in juveniles only), A. jishouensis, A. kreyenbergii, A. parallens, A. spinifer, A. wenchowensis, and A. wuyiensis.

The nominal species A. labiatus is currently considered synonymous with A. paradoxus according to some sources although this appears to be in question.
